metadata.title: Rear Triangle Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Rear Triangle Bottom position in BJJ. Defensive guide covering escape mechanics, counter-attacks, and survival strategies. Advanced escape rate 40%.

overview:
Rear Triangle Bottom is a highly compromised defensive position where the practitioner is caught in a triangle choke configuration applied from the opponent's back control position. This represents one of the most dangerous submission threats in BJJ, combining the control advantages of back mount with the finishing mechanics of the triangle choke. The bottom player faces significant constraints on mobility and breathing, with the opponent's legs creating a figure-four configuration around the neck and one arm while maintaining back control elements.

This position typically occurs when an opponent successfully transitions from standard back control or seated back mount into a triangle configuration, often catching one arm inside the triangle while controlling the back. The defensive player must navigate multiple submission threats including the triangle choke itself, potential transitions to armbars, and the ever-present danger of the rear naked choke. Understanding the escape hierarchy and maintaining composure under extreme pressure are essential for survival and eventual escape from this precarious position.
state_invariants: Opponent's legs are configured in a figure-four triangle formation around the defender's neck and one trapped arm, with the ankle locked behind the knee creating the choking mechanism
Defender's back is exposed to opponent with at least one arm trapped inside the triangle structure, severely limiting defensive hand fighting options and posture
Opponent maintains elements of back control including hooks or body triangle combined with the triangle configuration, creating a hybrid control position with multiple submission threats
Defender's head and trapped arm are enclosed within the triangle's loop with pressure being applied to the carotid arteries and increasing oxygen deprivation over time
prerequisites: Opponent successfully transitioned from back control or seated back mount to triangle configuration
One of defender's arms became trapped inside the triangle structure during the transition or initial control phase
Opponent secured the figure-four leg lock with ankle behind knee creating the triangle choking mechanism
Defender failed to prevent the triangle lock or immediately address the positional threat during the setup phase
key_principles: Immediately address posture and create space between head and choking leg to relieve carotid pressure and buy time
Focus on extracting the trapped arm from inside the triangle as the primary escape pathway before addressing other threats
Maintain chin protection by tucking chin to chest and turning face toward the non-choking leg side to reduce choke effectiveness
Control opponent's choking leg ankle or knee to prevent them from tightening the triangle and to create leverage for escape attempts
Stay calm and manage breathing despite restricted airway, avoiding panic that accelerates oxygen depletion and poor decision-making
Recognize submission sequences (triangle to armbar, triangle to back take) and defend transitions preemptively rather than reactively
Generate rotation and angle changes to disrupt the triangle's structure rather than attempting pure strength-based escapes

common_errors.error: Attempting to pull the head out first before addressing the trapped arm inside the triangle
common_errors.consequence: Opponent tightens triangle and angles hips to finish the choke more effectively, accelerating loss of consciousness
common_errors.correction: Focus all initial escape efforts on extracting the trapped arm from inside the triangle before attempting to remove the head

common_errors.error: Using pure strength to fight the triangle without creating angles or leverage points
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion while the opponent maintains control with minimal effort, leading to exhaustion and inevitable submission
common_errors.correction: Utilize strategic movements including rotation, hip movement, and grip fighting to create mechanical advantages rather than relying on muscular force

common_errors.error: Failing to protect the chin and turning the face toward the choking leg
common_errors.consequence: Significantly increased choke effectiveness as the carotid arteries become more exposed to compression, shortening time to unconsciousness
common_errors.correction: Immediately tuck chin to chest and turn face toward the non-choking leg to create a defensive structure that buys time for escape attempts

common_errors.error: Panicking and making erratic movements that assist the opponent's control and finishing mechanics
common_errors.consequence: Uncontrolled movements provide opportunities for opponent to adjust position, tighten the choke, or transition to alternative submissions
common_errors.correction: Maintain mental composure, breathe strategically through the restricted airway, and execute deliberate escape sequences methodically

common_errors.error: Ignoring the opponent's potential transitions to armbar or other submissions while focused solely on the triangle
common_errors.consequence: Getting caught in secondary submissions like armbars when the opponent transitions from the triangle during escape attempts
common_errors.correction: Maintain awareness of the entire submission chain including triangle-to-armbar transitions and defend multiple threats simultaneously

common_errors.error: Failing to control the opponent's choking leg ankle or knee during escape attempts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent freely adjusts leg position to optimize choke angle and pressure, preventing effective escape execution
common_errors.correction: Establish grip control on the choking leg's ankle or behind the knee to limit opponent's adjustments and create escape leverage

common_errors.error: Attempting to stand up or create large positional changes without first addressing the triangle structure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent rides the movement easily while maintaining or tightening the triangle, often transitioning to more dominant variations
common_errors.correction: Dismantle the triangle structure first through arm extraction and space creation before attempting major positional escapes

training_drills.name: Rear Triangle Survival Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies rear triangle with varying degrees of tightness while defender practices maintaining composure, chin protection, and controlled breathing for timed intervals (30-60 seconds). Focus on staying calm under pressure and recognizing the feeling of different triangle tightness levels before they become critical.

training_drills.name: Arm Extraction Repetition Drill
training_drills.description: Start with rear triangle partially locked and practice extracting the trapped arm using various hand grips, elbow positioning, and shoulder rotation techniques. Partner provides progressive resistance levels to build technical proficiency before speed and power application.

training_drills.name: Triangle Escape Sequence Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies rear triangle at 50-70% intensity while defender flows through complete escape sequences including arm extraction, posture recovery, and positional escape to turtle or guard recovery. Reset and repeat to build muscle memory for the complete defensive chain.

training_drills.name: Triangle to Submission Chain Defense
training_drills.description: Partner alternates between finishing the triangle, transitioning to armbar, and switching to rear naked choke while defender practices defending multiple submission threats simultaneously. Develops awareness of submission chains and transitions.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Rear Triangle Bottom
training_drills.description: Start in fully locked rear triangle bottom position with defender earning 1 point for successful arm extraction, 2 points for complete escape to neutral or better position. Attacker earns points for submission finish or maintaining control for 2+ minutes. First to 5 points wins.

expert_insights.danaher: The rear triangle bottom position represents a convergence of two of the most powerful control systems in grappling—the back control framework and the triangle choking mechanism. From a biomechanical perspective, the defender faces a dual constraint system where the legs create arterial compression while the back position limits rotational escape options. The key to survival lies in understanding the hierarchical nature of the escape sequence: first, you must address the trapped arm, as this is the structural weakness in the triangle configuration when applied from the back. The opponent's triangle is only as strong as their ability to maintain the arm inside, so your primary objective must be extraction of that limb through strategic hand positioning and elbow frames. Only after arm extraction should you attempt to address the choking leg itself. The systematic approach to defense requires maintaining chin protection throughout, controlling the choking leg's ankle or knee to limit opponent adjustments, and using small, precise movements rather than explosive panic-driven reactions. Remember that the opponent's position, while dominant, also constrains their own mobility—use this to your advantage by timing your escape attempts to moments when they adjust or transition between submissions.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Getting caught in a rear triangle is one of the worst positions you can find yourself in during competition, but I've escaped it enough times to know it's not automatically over if you keep your composure and work the right sequence. The first thing I focus on is protecting my chin and immediately grabbing that choking leg—usually at the ankle—because if I can control that leg, they can't adjust the angle to finish me. My trapped arm is the biggest problem, so I'm working to get that elbow down and start walking my hand across my body to extract it. Once that arm is out, the triangle starts falling apart and I can think about actually escaping rather than just surviving. The mistake I see people make is trying to use strength to just rip their head out, but that doesn't work against anyone good—they'll just tighten it up and finish you faster. Instead, I focus on small technical movements: hand fighting, controlling their legs, and creating just enough space to start the extraction process. In competition, I've found that staying calm and breathing efficiently through the restriction buys me the time I need to work my escapes systematically. If you panic and start thrashing, you're done. If you stay technical and work the positions, you can survive and escape even against high-level opponents who have locked this position in tight.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Rear triangle bottom is basically the ultimate nightmare scenario—you're getting strangled from a position where they have your back and one of your arms is trapped, so you're dealing with multiple problems at once. But here's the thing about the 10th Planet approach to this: we train this position specifically because it comes up in our game when we're hunting for back triangles ourselves, so we know both sides intimately. The key is understanding that the triangle from the back isn't quite as tight as a front triangle because the angle is different and they don't have as much hip mobility to squeeze. That's your window. You need to immediately control that choking leg—grab the ankle, grab behind the knee, whatever you can get—and start working to turn your face away from the choke toward their non-choking leg. Then you're working that trapped arm out by any means necessary: sliding the hand, dropping the elbow, rotating the shoulder. We drill this with the principle that you never give up on the arm extraction because once that arm is free, the whole structure collapses. I also teach my guys to look for the roll-through escape if the opponent's triangle isn't fully locked yet—sometimes you can use their own momentum against them if they're trying to finish too aggressively. The mental game is huge here too; you have to train yourself not to panic when the blood flow gets restricted. We do a lot of survival drilling where guys hold the position at different tightness levels so you get comfortable with that feeling and don't tap prematurely. It's all about staying creative, staying technical, and understanding that even the worst positions have escape routes if you know where to look.

metadata.title: Rear Triangle | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master the Rear Triangle position in BJJ. Advanced back control variation with 70% submission rate. Learn triangle mechanics from back control with expert insights.

overview:
The Rear Triangle is an advanced controlling position that combines the dominance of back control with the submission mechanics of a triangle choke. From back control, the attacker transitions one leg over the opponent's shoulder while maintaining back control fundamentals, creating a hybrid position that offers exceptional control and multiple high-percentage finishing opportunities.

This position represents one of the most dominant variations of back control, as it eliminates many standard defensive options while opening direct pathways to multiple submissions. The rear triangle creates structural control that prevents opponent rotation and escape while applying constant pressure to the neck and shoulder. Unlike standard back control where opponents can sometimes defend by tucking their chin or creating frames, the rear triangle's leg configuration creates a mechanical advantage that is extremely difficult to counter.

The position serves as both a control position and a submission position, making it a premier example of position-before-submission philosophy. Practitioners who master the rear triangle gain access to a systematic approach to back attacks that significantly increases their finishing rate from back control.
state_invariants: Attacker positioned on opponent's back with chest against opponent's upper back and shoulder blades, maintaining constant forward pressure
One leg (typically right leg) threaded over opponent's right shoulder with knee pointing upward, shin pressing across the front of opponent's neck and collarbone
Opposite leg (left leg) positioned behind opponent's head with foot placed in the crook of the right knee, completing the triangle configuration
At least one hook (inside leg control with foot on opponent's inner thigh) maintained on the non-triangle side to prevent opponent rotation
Arms controlling opponent's posture through collar grips, arm control, or seat belt grip (one arm over shoulder, one under armpit)
Opponent's head trapped between attacker's legs with limited ability to turn or rotate away from the triangle pressure
Attacker's hips elevated and positioned high on opponent's back, creating downward angle for triangle pressure while maintaining balance
prerequisites: Successful establishment of back control with hooks or body triangle
Control of opponent's upper body through seat belt, harness, or arm control
Opponent in defensive posture (typically sitting or on hands and knees)
Sufficient flexibility to thread leg over opponent's shoulder while maintaining back attachment
Opponent's arm isolated or controlled on the triangle side
Space created to bring knee over opponent's shoulder
key_principles: Maintain constant forward pressure with chest against opponent's back throughout triangle establishment
Keep triangle leg (shin) tight across opponent's neck, not just resting on shoulder
Squeeze knees together to tighten triangle configuration and increase neck pressure
Maintain at least one hook or control point to prevent opponent rotation away from triangle
Control opponent's near-side arm to prevent defensive frames and posture recovery
Keep hips elevated and mobile to adjust triangle angle based on opponent reactions
Combine triangle pressure with arm attacks to create multiple simultaneous threats

common_errors.error: Placing shin on opponent's shoulder instead of across their neck
common_errors.consequence: Creates no choking pressure and allows opponent to easily defend or escape by pulling shoulder away
common_errors.correction: Actively drive shin across the front of opponent's neck, ensuring direct contact with carotid arteries and trachea area

common_errors.error: Releasing bottom hook while establishing triangle
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to rotate their body away from triangle pressure and escape back control entirely
common_errors.correction: Maintain at least one hook throughout triangle establishment; only release second hook once triangle is locked and secure

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's near-side arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can create defensive frames, push against triangle leg, or recover posture to relieve pressure
common_errors.correction: Trap near-side arm with overhook, underhook, or wrist control before fully committing to triangle configuration

common_errors.error: Sitting back too far while attempting triangle
common_errors.consequence: Creates space between chest and opponent's back, allowing opponent to turn into guard or escape laterally
common_errors.correction: Maintain chest-to-back connection with forward pressure throughout triangle setup and finishing sequence

common_errors.error: Crossing feet in loose figure-four instead of tight triangle lock
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can push foot out of knee crook, breaking triangle configuration and escaping control
common_errors.correction: Ensure foot is deeply locked in opposite knee's crook with toes pulled toward shin for maximum security

common_errors.error: Attempting triangle on wrong side (side without arm isolation)
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses free arm to create frames and defensive structures that prevent triangle completion
common_errors.correction: Set up triangle only on side where opponent's arm is controlled or trapped beneath your body

common_errors.error: Keeping hips flat instead of elevated during triangle application
common_errors.consequence: Reduces choking angle and pressure, making triangle less effective and easier to defend
common_errors.correction: Elevate hips and create downward angle with triangle, using body weight to increase pressure on neck

expert_insights.danaher: The rear triangle represents a biomechanical perfection in controlling an opponent from the back position. What makes this position particularly effective is the structural control it provides - the triangle configuration creates a closed kinetic chain that eliminates the opponent's ability to rotate away from danger. The mechanics are superior to standard back control because your legs create a more powerful squeeze than your arms ever could, while simultaneously freeing your hands to attack. The key technical detail most practitioners miss is the shin position - it must cross the neck at the carotid level, not rest on the shoulder. When executing the rear triangle, think of it as creating a vice where your legs are the primary control mechanism and your arms provide secondary controls that set up submission opportunities. The position also creates what I call a 'submission nexus' - a point where multiple high-percentage attacks converge, making defensive decision-making extremely difficult for your opponent.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the rear triangle is one of my highest-percentage positions because it eliminates so many of the standard back escape options opponents typically rely on. When I lock up the rear triangle, I immediately notice opponents panic because they can feel they're in serious danger but their usual defensive frames don't work. The position is particularly effective in no-gi where you can't rely on collar grips for control. My focus is always on using the triangle as a control position first, not rushing the finish. I maintain the rear triangle for 10-15 seconds, let my opponent exhaust themselves trying to defend, then choose my attack based on what they give me. If they try to posture up or frame, I immediately switch to the armbar. If they tuck their chin hard and pull their head down, I'll often release the triangle and slide my arm under for the RNC. The key is recognizing that the rear triangle creates such good control that you can be patient and wait for the perfect finishing opportunity rather than forcing a lower-percentage submission.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The rear triangle is a beautiful position because it combines the control elements we love in 10th Planet with multiple submission paths. From a rubber guard and truck background, I approach the rear triangle differently than traditional back control - I use it as a transition position to create chaos and force reactions. When I lock up the rear triangle, I'm immediately thinking about calf slicers, crucifix transitions, and even twister setups if the opponent tries to roll. The flexibility required for the rear triangle is significant, which is why we emphasize daily stretching in our system. One variation I teach that's particularly effective is using the rear triangle as a control position while you work on isolating the far arm for the crucifix - the triangle prevents them from rotating away while you trap the far arm. Don't sleep on the near-side armbar from this position either - when they frame against the triangle, their arm is perfectly positioned for you to swing over into a belly-down armbar. The rear triangle is also excellent for setting up the truck position if your opponent manages to start turning into you.

metadata.title: Rear Triangle Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Rear Triangle Top position in BJJ. Control opponent's back with triangle legs configuration. Advanced 4-point position with 70% submission rate from back attacks.

overview:
Rear Triangle Top is an advanced back control variation where the top practitioner secures the opponent's back while establishing a triangle configuration with their legs around the opponent's body and one arm. This position combines the control elements of traditional back control with the limb-trapping mechanics of a triangle, creating a highly effective submission platform. The rear triangle creates a dilemma for the opponent - defending the choke exposes the trapped arm to attacks, while defending the arm allows progression to the rear naked choke or other back attacks. This position is particularly effective in no-gi grappling but can be equally devastating in the gi when properly executed.

The rear triangle top position represents a sophisticated evolution of back control, offering superior control compared to standard seat belt positioning. By threading one leg under the opponent's armpit and locking a triangle around their neck and trapped arm, the top practitioner creates multiple layers of control that significantly reduce the opponent's defensive options. This position is often entered from standard back control when the opponent attempts to defend the rear naked choke by gripping their own hands together or when transitioning from turtle position. The configuration allows for seamless transitions to various submissions including the rear triangle choke itself, armbar variations, and traditional rear naked choke finishes.

From a strategic perspective, the rear triangle top position exemplifies the principle of creating submission dilemmas - forcing the opponent to choose between equally bad defensive options. The position's effectiveness stems from its ability to control the opponent's posture, limit their mobility, and create multiple simultaneous threats. Advanced practitioners use this position to systematically break down defensive structures, often cycling through submission attempts to create openings. The position requires significant technical knowledge and body awareness to maintain effectively, making it primarily a blue belt and above technique, though competition-focused practitioners may encounter it earlier in their training.
state_invariants: Top practitioner's legs form a triangle configuration around opponent's neck and one trapped arm, with one leg threaded under the armpit and across the back of the neck while the other leg locks over the ankle to complete the triangle

Top practitioner maintains chest-to-back connection with their torso pressed against opponent's back, hips oriented toward the trapped arm side to maximize control and create the optimal angle for submissions
Opponent is typically seated or on their side with one arm trapped inside the triangle while their body is compressed forward by the leg pressure across their neck and shoulder
Top practitioner's hands are free to attack the opponent's free arm, establish grips for chokes, or post for base while the legs maintain primary control of the position

The triangle configuration creates constant pressure on the opponent's carotid artery on the trapped arm side while controlling their posture and preventing them from turning into the top practitioner
prerequisites: Established back control position with hooks or body triangle
Opponent's defensive hand fighting creates opportunity to trap one arm
Sufficient hip mobility and leg dexterity to thread leg under opponent's armpit
Understanding of triangle mechanics and proper leg positioning
Ability to maintain back control during the transition to triangle configuration
Opponent positioned in seated or side-lying orientation allowing leg threading
key_principles: Thread the choking leg deep under the opponent's armpit to create proper angle across the back of their neck rather than the front
Lock the triangle tight by pulling the locking ankle into the crook of the knee while squeezing knees together to compress the opponent's neck and trapped arm
Maintain chest pressure against opponent's back throughout the position to prevent them from turning into you or creating space
Control opponent's free arm with your hands to prevent defensive gripping and create additional submission opportunities
Angle your hips toward the trapped arm side to increase pressure on the carotid artery and create better finishing mechanics for the choke
Use your legs to break opponent's posture forward, bringing their chin to their chest to tighten the choke and reduce defensive options
Transition fluidly between submission threats - rear triangle choke, armbar on trapped arm, and rear naked choke - to overwhelm opponent's defenses

common_errors.error: Threading leg in front of opponent's neck instead of behind, creating a front triangle configuration
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily defend by tucking chin and the choke pressure is significantly reduced
common_errors.correction: Thread the leg deep under the armpit so it emerges behind the opponent's neck, creating proper back triangle mechanics

common_errors.error: Locking the triangle too loosely without proper compression of knees together
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can create space, potentially pull trapped arm free, or escape the position entirely
common_errors.correction: Pull the locking ankle tightly into the crook of the knee and actively squeeze knees together to eliminate all space

common_errors.error: Losing chest-to-back connection by sitting up too far or leaning away from opponent
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can turn into you, potentially escaping to guard or reversing the position
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant chest pressure against opponent's back with your weight committed forward onto them

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's free arm, allowing them to establish defensive grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can grab their own leg to prevent triangle lock or defend against choke finishing attempts
common_errors.correction: Use your hands to control the free arm by wrist control, overhook, or isolating it away from defensive positions

common_errors.error: Not angling hips sufficiently toward trapped arm side
common_errors.consequence: Reduced pressure on the carotid artery and less effective choke mechanics
common_errors.correction: Actively angle your hips and shoulders toward the trapped arm to create optimal cutting angle across the neck

common_errors.error: Abandoning position too quickly when opponent defends initial choke attempt
common_errors.consequence: Missing opportunities to attack multiple submissions and cycle through finishing options
common_errors.correction: Systematically cycle between rear triangle choke, armbar on trapped arm, and rear naked choke to break down defenses

training_drills.name: Triangle Entry from Back Control Drill
training_drills.description: Start in standard back control with seat belt grip. Partner defends by gripping hands together. Practice threading your leg under their armpit and locking the triangle configuration while maintaining back control. Repeat 10 times each side, focusing on smooth entry without losing position. Partner should provide realistic defensive resistance but allow successful entries.

training_drills.name: Submission Cycling Drill
training_drills.description: Establish rear triangle top position. Flow continuously between rear triangle choke attempt, armbar on trapped arm, and rear naked choke for 3-minute rounds. Partner defends each attempt realistically, forcing you to transition between submissions. Focus on maintaining position control throughout all transitions. Reset if position is lost.

training_drills.name: Position Maintenance Under Pressure
training_drills.description: Partner starts in rear triangle bottom position and uses full effort to escape for 2 minutes while you focus solely on maintaining the position without finishing submissions. Partner should attempt various escapes: turning in, bridging, pulling trapped arm free, creating space. Your goal is to keep the triangle locked and maintain back connection throughout.

training_drills.name: Triangle Lock Tightness Progression
training_drills.description: Establish rear triangle position with compliant partner. Practice the following progression: lock triangle loosely (30 seconds), medium tightness (30 seconds), maximum compression (30 seconds). Partner provides feedback on pressure levels. Focus on understanding the difference in control at each compression level. Repeat for 5 cycles per side.

expert_insights.danaher: The rear triangle represents a sophisticated evolution in back attack methodology, combining the leg control mechanics of the triangle with the positional dominance of back control. The critical technical element that separates effective rear triangle application from ineffective attempts is the angle of the choking leg - it must thread deeply under the armpit and emerge behind the neck, not in front. This creates what I call a 'posterior triangle configuration' which applies pressure to the back and side of the neck rather than the front, making chin-tucking defenses largely ineffective. The position's true power lies in its ability to create submission dilemmas - when the opponent defends the choke by addressing the trapped arm, they expose the neck to rear naked choke attacks; when they defend the neck, they expose the trapped arm to armbars and shoulder locks. This systematic approach to creating and exploiting dilemmas is the hallmark of advanced back attack methodology.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I use the rear triangle extensively in competition because it's one of the highest-percentage back control variations when you're facing elite defensive grapplers who are excellent at defending the standard rear naked choke. The key to success with this position in high-level competition is the entry - you need to establish the triangle during a defensive reaction, typically when they're hand-fighting and trying to prevent your choking hand from going under their chin. That's when their arm is most exposed for the triangle trap. Once I have the rear triangle locked, I never commit to one submission - I'm constantly cycling between the triangle choke itself, the armbar on the trapped arm, and coming back to the rear naked choke. This creates massive mental and physical fatigue in the opponent because they're defending multiple threats simultaneously. In my matches, the rear triangle has about a 70% finish rate within 90 seconds because opponents simply can't maintain adequate defenses against all the submission options.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The rear triangle is one of those positions that perfectly exemplifies the 10th Planet philosophy of creating inescapable submission traps through unconventional positioning. We call this the 'Rear Triangle Prison' because once it's locked in tight, there's really no good escape - every defensive movement the opponent makes opens up a different submission. What makes this position especially effective in no-gi is that without the gi grips to defend with, opponents are forced to rely purely on their own body positioning, which we control completely with the triangle configuration. I teach my students to enter the rear triangle whenever they feel the opponent starting to successfully defend the traditional back attacks - it's like shifting gears into a submission platform that most people haven't developed comprehensive defenses for. The beauty of it is that you can hold this position almost indefinitely while you work your submissions, and unlike some other back control variations, you're not burning your arms out trying to finish chokes - your legs are doing all the control work while your hands are free to attack.
